analogy.p: Imagine each halogen atom is a goalkeeper who needs **exactly one more ball** to be complete. A small goalkeeper (fluorine) stands close to a powerful magnet, the nucleus, so any ball that comes near is snatched instantly. A huge goalkeeper (iodine) has many layers of players (inner electron shells) between the ball and the magnet, which block the pull, so the ball is caught less eagerly. That is why reactivity falls as the atoms get bigger and why a more reactive halogen steals an electron from a less reactive halide ion. The analogy breaks down because real electrons are not caught like balls: they are attracted by electrostatic forces and the shells are not physical barriers, they only reduce the effective pull through shielding.
analogy.t: The halogens as people queuing to catch a ball

bullets: **Fluorine (F)**, **chlorine (Cl)**, **bromine (Br)** and **iodine (I)** are the four you must know in detail; **astatine (At)** is radioactive, rare and is only ever predicted from trends at GCSE.
Atomic numbers (the number of protons) are F = 9, Cl = 17, Br = 35, I = 53 and At = 85, so each element down the group has more electrons and more shells than the one above.
Electronic structures: F 2,7; Cl 2,8,7; Br 2,8,18,7; I 2,8,18,18,7. The **last number is always 7**, which is why they are in the same group.
The name 'halogen' means 'salt former' because they react with metals to make **salts** such as sodium chloride and potassium bromide.
**Group number = number of outer electrons** is the rule that links the periodic table to electronic structure, and it is the reason elements in a group react in a similar way.
The halogens are found on the right of the periodic table, so they are non-metals with low melting points compared with metals, and they do not conduct electricity.
core.h: 1. Where the halogens are and what 'Group 7' means
core.p: The **halogens** are the elements in **Group 7** of the periodic table, the second column from the right, next to the noble gases in Group 0. The group number tells you the number of electrons in the outer shell, so every halogen atom has **7 outer shell electrons**. The AQA specification names fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine and expects you to predict the properties of others (such as astatine) from the trends. All halogens are **non-metals**, which is why their properties are so different from the metals you meet in Group 1.

bullets: To obtain a full outer shell with a stable noble gas arrangement, a halogen atom gains **1 electron** and forms a **1- ion** (for example F-, Cl-, Br-, I-).
These ions are called **halide ions**; the individual names are fluoride, chloride, bromide and iodide. Note the ending '-ide' for the ion compared with '-ine' for the element.
In reactions with **metals**, electrons are **transferred** from the metal to the halogen, so **ionic bonds** form.
In reactions with **non-metals**, electrons are **shared** so **covalent bonds** form (for example HCl, or the Cl-Cl bond itself).
A halogen atom gaining an electron is **reduction** (gain of electrons); this is the Higher tier idea needed for displacement reactions.
Group 7 elements **gain** electrons whereas Group 1 elements **lose** electrons: always compare the two groups when asked about trends in reactivity, because the explanations are opposites.
core.h: 2. Why the halogens react similarly: electronic structure
core.p: Chemical reactions involve the outer shell electrons. All halogens are **one electron short of a full outer shell**, so each atom is highly keen either to **gain one electron** (forming a negative ion) or to **share one electron** (forming a covalent bond). Because they all have the same number of outer electrons, they all follow the same pattern of reactions, even though the speed (reactivity) changes down the group. This is exactly the same reasoning as for Group 1, where elements with 1 outer electron all lose it to form 1+ ions.

bullets: Formulas: always write the halogen elements as **F2, Cl2, Br2, I2**, not as single atoms. A mark is often lost for writing 'Cl' instead of 'Cl2'.

**Fluorine** is a pale yellow gas; **chlorine** is a pale green gas (AQA also describes it as a fairly reactive, poisonous green gas); **bromine** is a red-brown volatile liquid; **iodine** is a dark grey crystalline solid that gives a purple vapour when warmed.
Examiners accept 'fluorine: very pale yellow gas', 'chlorine: green gas', 'bromine: orange-brown liquid' and 'iodine: grey/black solid'; learn the physical state and colour as a pair.
**Volatile** means evaporates easily. Bromine is described as volatile because it gives off a brown-orange vapour even at room temperature.

The values at normal pressure are approximately: melting points F2 -220 C, Cl2 -101 C, Br2 -7 C, I2 114 C; boiling points F2 -188 C, Cl2 -34 C, Br2 59 C, I2 184 C. You do not have to learn the numbers but should be able to use them to decide the state at a given temperature.
Because room temperature is about 20 C: gases if boiling point is below 20 C, liquid if the melting point is below 20 C and the boiling point above 20 C, solid if the melting point is above 20 C.
All halogen elements are **poor conductors of electricity** because they have no free electrons or ions to carry charge.
core.p: The halogens exist as **diatomic molecules**, meaning two atoms joined by a single **covalent bond**: F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2. Each atom shares one electron with the other so that both have a full outer shell of 8 electrons. Because they are small covalent molecules, they have **low melting and boiling points** compared with ionic compounds or metals, they do not conduct electricity, and the strength of the forces **between** molecules decides the state at room temperature.

bullets: Down the group, the **relative molecular mass** increases: F2 = 38, Cl2 = 71, Br2 = 160, I2 = 254 (using Ar F = 19, Cl = 35.5, Br = 80, I = 127).
Bigger molecules have **stronger intermolecular forces**, so melting and boiling need more energy and happen at higher temperatures.

**Key exam point:** when a halogen melts or boils, it is the weak **intermolecular forces** that are overcome, **not** the covalent bonds between the atoms in each molecule. Saying that covalent bonds break loses the mark.
The covalent bond inside the molecule is strong; this is why simple molecular substances still have low melting points: only the weak forces between molecules need breaking.
This trend lets you **predict**: astatine (At2) should be a **solid** with a **higher melting and boiling point than iodine**, and it is expected to be darker (black).
Likewise fluorine, at the top, has the lowest melting and boiling points of the group and is a gas.
Data question tip: if a table gives melting points, describe the trend with numbers, e.g. 'increases from -101 C for chlorine to 114 C for iodine'.
core.h: 4. Trend: melting and boiling points increase down the group
core.p: Going down Group 7 the melting point and boiling point **increase**. This is why the state changes from gas (F2, Cl2) to liquid (Br2) to solid (I2). The explanation is about **intermolecular forces**, not about the strong covalent bond inside each molecule. Larger molecules have more electrons, so the forces of attraction between the molecules are stronger, and **more energy is needed to overcome them**.

bullets: **Step 1:** halogen atoms react by gaining 1 electron in the outer shell.
**Step 2:** going down, atoms have more electron shells, so the outer shell is **further from the nucleus**.
**Step 3:** more inner shells means **more shielding** of the outer shell from the positive nucleus.
**Step 4:** so the **force of attraction** between the nucleus and the electron to be gained is **weaker**, and the atom gains an electron **less easily**.
**Result:** reactivity decreases from F to I, so F is the most reactive and I is least reactive of the four.

Compare Group 1: the outer electron is **lost** and is lost more easily further down, so reactivity **increases** down Group 1. In Group 7 the electron is **gained**, and it is gained less easily further down.
Reactivity of the halogens shows up experimentally in how readily they react with iron wool (fluorine and chlorine react vigorously, bromine less so, iodine slowly) and in displacement reactions.
Use the words **'outer shell', 'further from the nucleus', 'more shielding', 'weaker attraction', 'gain an electron'** in six mark answers; they are the mark scheme phrases.
core.h: 5. Trend: reactivity decreases down the group (Higher tier explanation)
core.p: Reactivity in Group 7 **decreases** as you go **down** the group, the opposite of Group 1. Fluorine is the most reactive halogen and reacts violently with most elements, whereas iodine is much less reactive. The reason is that a halogen atom reacts by **gaining** one electron into its outer shell. Down the group the outer shell is **further from the nucleus** and there is **more shielding** from the inner shells, so the **attraction between the nucleus and the incoming electron is weaker**, and the electron is gained less easily.

bullets: **Sodium + chlorine:** 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl (sodium chloride). Sodium burns with a bright yellow-orange flame in chlorine and forms a white solid.
**Iron wool + chlorine:** 2Fe + 3Cl2 → 2FeCl3 (iron(III) chloride, a brown solid). Chlorine is a strong enough oxidising agent to give Fe3+, not Fe2+.
Naming rule: the halogen part of the name ends in **-ide**: sodium chloride, potassium bromide, magnesium iodide, calcium fluoride.
Metal atom → positive ion (loses electrons); halogen atom → halide ion X- (gains one electron). The charges must balance, so the group 2 metal magnesium reacts: Mg + Cl2 → MgCl2.
Simple formula pattern: the halide is 1-, so a group 1 metal gives MX, group 2 gives MX2, and aluminium (3+) gives AlX3.
The reaction is **vigorous** with fluorine and chlorine and increasingly slower down the group, linking back to the reactivity trend.
Ionic halides dissolve in water to give colourless solutions (for example NaCl, KBr, KI), which are the solutions used in displacement reactions.
core.h: 6. Reactions with metals: forming ionic halides
core.p: Halogens react with metals to form **metal halides**, which are **ionic compounds**. Each halogen atom gains one electron from the metal to become a **halide ion** with a 1- charge, and the metal loses electrons to become a positive ion. The ions are held together by strong **electrostatic forces of attraction** in a giant ionic lattice. These compounds are called salts and are generally white crystalline solids with high melting points that conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved.

bullets: **Hydrogen + chlorine:** H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl (hydrogen chloride). Hydrogen + fluorine: H2 + F2 → 2HF; hydrogen + bromine: H2 + Br2 → 2HBr; hydrogen + iodine: H2 + I2 → 2HI.
In HCl there is a **single covalent bond**, a shared pair of electrons, between H and Cl.

The reaction of fluorine with hydrogen is explosive even in the dark, chlorine needs a light source or flame to start, bromine and iodine react more slowly, which again shows the reactivity trend (mention only if comparing trends).
Other covalent compounds with non-metals include chlorine with carbon (such as CCl4) and with phosphorus, but the key AQA examples are the hydrogen halides.
Covalent molecules have **low melting and boiling points** because of weak intermolecular forces, and they do **not conduct electricity** because there are no ions or free electrons.
Always distinguish: **metal + halogen = ionic**, **non-metal + halogen = covalent**. This is a very commonly tested bonding link.
core.h: 7. Reactions with non-metals: forming covalent molecules
core.p: When halogens react with **non-metals** the atoms **share electrons** to form **simple covalent molecules**. The best example is the reaction with hydrogen, which makes the **hydrogen halides**. In each hydrogen halide molecule, one shared pair of electrons joins the hydrogen atom and the halogen atom so that both have a full outer shell. Hydrogen halides are small molecules, so they are **gases at room temperature**.

bullets: Equation with state symbols: HCl(g) → H+(aq) + Cl-(aq) when dissolved in water. The solution of hydrogen chloride in water is **hydrochloric acid**.
The solution has a **low pH (pH below 7)**, turns universal indicator red/orange and blue litmus paper red.
Similarly hydrogen fluoride gives hydrofluoric acid, hydrogen bromide gives hydrobromic acid and hydrogen iodide gives hydroiodic acid.
The **covalent** molecule HCl has no ions in the pure gas; the ions form only because water molecules help the molecule to ionise. Dry HCl gas does not show acidic properties in the same way.
Hydrochloric acid is a **strong acid** in the sense that it is fully ionised in water (full ionisation is Higher tier, in the acids section).
Because the HCl gas dissolves very readily, this is a fact used in the fountain experiment and in explaining why HCl gas gives misty fumes in damp air.
Link to other topics: hydrochloric acid reacts with metals, bases, alkalis and carbonates to make **chloride salts**.
core.h: 8. Hydrogen halides dissolve in water to form acidic solutions
core.p: The hydrogen halides are **molecular gases**, but when they dissolve in water they **ionise** (split up into ions) and make **acidic solutions**. Hydrogen chloride gas dissolves to form **hydrochloric acid**. The acidity comes from the **hydrogen ions (H+)** released. This links directly to the acids topic, where an acid is a substance that forms H+ ions in aqueous solution.

bullets: **Method:** add a few cm3 of the halogen solution (chlorine water, bromine water or iodine solution) to a few cm3 of the potassium halide solution in a test tube or spotting tile, and observe any colour change.
**Chlorine water + potassium bromide:** solution turns from colourless to **orange** because bromine is formed. Chlorine + potassium bromide → potassium chloride + bromine: Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2.
**Chlorine water + potassium iodide:** solution turns **brown** because iodine is formed: Cl2 + 2KI → 2KCl + I2.
**Bromine water + potassium iodide:** turns **brown**: Br2 + 2KI → 2KBr + I2.
**Bromine water + potassium chloride**, **iodine + potassium chloride** and **iodine + potassium bromide** show **no reaction** (no colour change) because the added halogen is less reactive.
In word equations name the salts: chlorine + sodium bromide → sodium chloride + bromine.
Safety: chlorine and bromine are **toxic** and **corrosive**, so use dilute solutions (halogen water), wear eye protection and gloves, and work in a **fume cupboard** or well ventilated area.
Interpretation: if the colour of the halogen being added is the colour you see at the end, no new halogen was made, so no displacement happened; a **new colour** means displacement.
core.p: A more reactive halogen will **displace** a less reactive halogen from a solution of its **halide salt**. For example, chlorine will displace bromine from potassium bromide solution, because chlorine is more reactive than bromine. A less reactive halogen cannot displace a more reactive one, so there is no reaction. These reactions provide direct experimental evidence for the order of reactivity Cl > Br > I.

bullets: Full equation: Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2. Ionic equation: **Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2**. The **K+ ions are spectator ions**, they are unchanged and are left out.
Half equation for reduction (electron gain): **Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl-**. Chlorine is **reduced** (it is the oxidising agent).
Half equation for oxidation (electron loss): **2Br- → Br2 + 2e-**. Bromide ions are **oxidised** (they are the reducing agent).
Chlorine with iodide: Cl2 + 2I- → 2Cl- + I2 (half equations Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl- and 2I- → I2 + 2e-).
Bromine with iodide: Br2 + 2I- → 2Br- + I2.
Check that the equation balances for **atoms** and for **charge**: left side Cl2 + 2Br- has total charge 2-, right side 2Cl- + Br2 has total charge 2-.
The more reactive halogen is the one that gains electrons more easily, so it is the better oxidising agent and takes electrons from the halide ion of the less reactive halogen.
Compare with metal displacement: more reactive metals displace less reactive metals (they lose electrons), whereas more reactive halogens displace less reactive halogens (they gain electrons).
core.h: 10. Displacement as redox: ionic equations and half equations (Higher tier)
core.p: Displacement reactions are **redox reactions**: one substance is **reduced** (gains electrons) while another is **oxidised** (loses electrons). In the reaction of chlorine with bromide ions, chlorine molecules **gain electrons** and bromide ions **lose electrons**. Writing the **ionic equation** removes the spectator ions (potassium ions, which are the same on both sides), leaving only the particles that change. Remember OIL RIG: **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss, **R**eduction **I**s **G**ain of electrons.

bullets: **Astatine (At2):** predicted to be a **black solid** at room temperature, with a **higher melting point and boiling point than iodine**, and **less reactive** than iodine.
Astatine would react with sodium to form sodium astatide, NaAt, an ionic compound containing the At- ion; it forms a hydrogen halide HAt covalent molecule.
Astatine would **not displace** iodine from potassium iodide, because it is less reactive than iodine; iodine **would** displace astatine from potassium astatide.
**Fluorine (F2):** the most reactive halogen, reacts violently with almost everything, and would displace **all** the other halogens from their salts.
The colour gets **darker** down the group: pale yellow, pale green, red-brown, dark grey/purple, black (predicted).
Predictions about states: if a question gives that bromine is a liquid and iodine a solid, then a halogen below iodine must also be a solid.
When predicting a melting point, give a value higher than the one above in the table and avoid exact values unless data supports it.
core.h: 11. Predicting properties from trends: fluorine and astatine
core.p: The specification says you should be able to **predict the properties of halogens from trends** and from data. Use the pattern down the group rather than memorising extra facts. Always say 'from the trend' in your answer, and state the direction of change (increases/decreases) plus a specific prediction.

bullets: **Test for chlorine:** hold **damp blue litmus paper** in the gas. It first turns red (chlorine dissolves to make an acidic solution) and is then **bleached white**. Dry litmus paper is not bleached.
**Hazards:** chlorine is toxic and harmful by inhalation, bromine is toxic and corrosive, iodine is harmful and stains the skin; all need careful handling.
**Uses (context):** chlorine is added to drinking water to kill microorganisms (sterilising), used in making bleach and plastics such as PVC.

Chlorine is made on a large scale by **electrolysis of brine (sodium chloride solution)**, where it forms at the **positive electrode (anode)** along with hydrogen at the cathode and sodium hydroxide solution.

**Chemistry only (triple):** halide ions can be identified using **silver nitrate** solution with dilute nitric acid: chloride gives a **white** precipitate, bromide a **cream** precipitate and iodide a **yellow** precipitate.
The ionic equation Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) → AgCl(s) shows the precipitation reaction; nitric acid is added first to remove carbonate ions that would also form a precipitate.
core.p: Chlorine is the halogen you meet most often. It is a **toxic, pungent gas** that irritates the respiratory system, so reactions must be done in a **fume cupboard**. It has an important test, bleaching damp litmus paper, and it is used in water treatment. These applications link the group to chemical analysis and the Earth's resources topics.

bullets: Link to **Group 1:** Group 1 metals lose 1 electron, reactivity **increases** down; Group 7 non-metals gain 1 electron, reactivity **decreases** down. Draw both trends side by side.
Link to **Group 0:** halogens are one electron short of the noble gas arrangement; noble gases are unreactive because their outer shell is already full.
Link to **ionic bonding:** metal halides are giant ionic lattices; the formula depends on the charge on the metal ion.
Link to **simple molecules:** diatomic halogens and the hydrogen halides are simple covalent, so low boiling points and no electrical conductivity.
Link to **electrolysis:** halide ions are discharged at the anode, forming the halogen, for example chlorine from sodium chloride solution.
Link to **organic chemistry:** chlorine and bromine are used in tests (bromine water for alkenes is in organic chemistry), and the chloro- prefix names halogenoalkanes (beyond GCSE).
Always give **state symbols** if asked and use '**displaces**' not 'replaces' or 'pushes out' in the more careful mark scheme language.
core.h: 13. Linking to other topics and exam strategy
core.p: Group 7 is a popular exam topic because it connects **bonding** (ionic vs covalent), **periodic table trends**, **redox**, **rates of reaction** and **chemical tests**. Mark schemes for 6 mark questions on this topic look for a logical chain of ideas: structure of atoms → electron gain → trend. Revising these links will help you answer unfamiliar contexts.

exam: **Command words:** 'State' = 1 fact (e.g. 'bromine is a red-brown liquid'); 'Describe' = what you see or the pattern; 'Explain' = give the reason using the structure; 'Predict' = use the trend and say the trend.
**1 mark:** state the colour or state of a halogen, the number of outer electrons (7), or the formula of the ion (e.g. Cl-).
**2 mark trend questions:** direction + data, e.g. 'melting point increases down the group, from -101 C for chlorine to 114 C for iodine'.
**2 mark explain melting point:** 'larger molecules / stronger intermolecular forces / more energy needed to overcome them' (and not covalent bonds breaking).
**Displacement observation (2 marks):** name the starting colour and the final colour of the solution, and say which halogen has been formed, e.g. 'colourless to orange; bromine formed'.
**3 mark equation questions:** word equation, balanced symbol equation with Cl2, or an ionic equation (Higher). Check charge and atoms balance.
**4 mark Higher tier:** explain displacement in terms of electrons: chlorine gains electrons (reduced), bromide ions lose electrons (oxidised), chlorine more reactive.

**6 mark reactivity answer:** structure the answer in a chain: outer shell electrons 7 → gain 1 electron → down the group more shells, further from nucleus, more shielding → weaker attraction → harder to gain → less reactive; give an example such as chlorine displacing bromine.
**Data tip:** in tables of results, 'no reaction' occurs when the halogen added is less reactive than the halogen in the salt; look for the diagonal pattern.
**Use the exact words:** 'displaces', 'more reactive', 'halide ions', 'outer shell', 'electrons are gained', 'intermolecular forces' for mark scheme credit.

mistakes.r: When simple molecules melt or boil, the weak intermolecular forces are overcome; the strong covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.
mistakes.w: Chlorine melts when the covalent bonds between the atoms break.

mistakes.r: Reactivity decreases down Group 7 because the outer shell is further from the nucleus with more shielding, so an electron is gained less easily.
mistakes.w: Reactivity increases down Group 7, as in Group 1.

mistakes.r: Halogens are diatomic: Cl2, Br2, I2 (and F2). The equation must balance with the molecular formulas.
mistakes.w: Writing the halogens as Cl, Br, I in equations.

mistakes.r: Only a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one; chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so bromine does not displace chlorine.
mistakes.w: Bromine will displace chlorine from sodium chloride.

mistakes.r: Halogens gain one electron to form 1- halide ions; Group 1 metals form 1+ ions.
Chlorine is the element (Cl2); chloride is the ion (Cl-) in compounds such as sodium chloride.
Iodine in aqueous solution is brown; solid iodine is dark grey and its vapour is purple.
Halogens with metals give ionic compounds; with non-metals they give covalent molecules.
mistakes.w: Ionic compounds are formed when halogens react with non-metals.

mistakes.r: Bromide ions lose electrons so they are oxidised; chlorine gains electrons so it is reduced.
mistakes.w: In the displacement ionic equation Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2, the bromide ions are reduced.

summary: The spec asks you to know the Group 7 halogens as diatomic non-metals with 7 outer electrons, their physical properties and trends (melting and boiling points rise, reactivity falls), their reactions with metals, non-metals and hydrogen, displacement reactions and (Higher) the electronic explanation and ionic equations. It matters because the halogens link bonding, periodicity and redox and appear regularly in 6 mark questions.

terms.d: An element in Group 7 of the periodic table; a non-metal with seven electrons in its outer shell.
A molecule made of two atoms joined by a covalent bond, such as Cl2.
A negative ion with a 1- charge formed when a halogen atom gains one electron, e.g. Cl-, Br-, I-.
A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
How readily a substance undergoes chemical reactions; for halogens it decreases down the group.
A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice.
Weak forces of attraction between simple molecules; overcome when a simple covalent substance melts or boils.
The effect of inner electron shells in reducing the attraction between the nucleus and the outer shell electrons.
The gain of electrons (OIL RIG: reduction is gain).
The loss of electrons (OIL RIG: oxidation is loss).
An equation showing only the ions or particles that take part in a reaction, leaving out spectator ions.
An equation showing the loss or gain of electrons by one species in a redox reaction, e.g. Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl-.
An ion that is present but does not change during a reaction, so it is omitted from the ionic equation.
A substance that evaporates easily at room temperature, such as bromine.
A covalent compound of hydrogen with a halogen, such as HCl, that dissolves in water to form an acidic solution.
A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal, or when a metal reacts with a halogen, e.g. sodium chloride.

worked.ans: Brown solution; chlorine is more reactive than iodine so displaces it; ionic equation: Cl2 + 2I- → 2Cl- + I2.
worked.q: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution. (a) State what you would see. (b) Explain why this happens. (c) Write the ionic equation. [5 marks]
steps: (a) The solution changes from colourless to **brown** (1 mark) because iodine is formed.
(b) Chlorine is **more reactive** than iodine (1 mark), so it **displaces** iodine from the potassium iodide (1 mark).
(c) Remove the spectator K+ ions from Cl2 + 2KI → 2KCl + I2 to get the ionic equation (1 mark for correct species).
Check balance: charge on left = 2- (from 2I-), charge on right = 2- (from 2Cl-); atoms: 2 Cl, 2 I on each side.

worked.ans: Both gain 1 electron into the outer shell. Fluorine has fewer shells, so the outer shell is closer to the nucleus and is less shielded, so the attraction to an incoming electron is stronger and the electron is gained more easily. Iodine has more shells, the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the attraction is weaker and an electron is gained less easily. Therefore fluorine is more reactive than iodine.
worked.q: Explain why fluorine is more reactive than iodine. [6 marks]
steps: Start with the electrons: both have seven electrons in the outer shell and react by gaining one electron.
Fluorine atoms are smaller, with fewer electron shells.
The outer shell is closer to the nucleus and there is less shielding.
So the attraction between the nucleus and the electron to be gained is stronger in fluorine.
So fluorine gains an electron more easily; in iodine the outer shell is further from the nucleus with more shielding, so the attraction is weaker.
Conclude that fluorine is more reactive than iodine.

worked.q: 2.3 g of sodium reacts completely with chlorine to make sodium chloride. Calculate the mass of sodium chloride formed. (Ar: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5) [3 marks]
steps: Moles of Na = mass ÷ Ar = 2.3 ÷ 23 = 0.10 mol.
Ratio Na : NaCl is 2 : 2 = 1 : 1, so moles of NaCl = 0.10 mol.
Check by conservation of mass: chlorine needed = 0.05 mol × 71 = 3.55 g; 2.3 + 3.55 = 5.85 g.
